items.originalTitle: France fires upgraded nuclear-capable missile from submarine for first time
items.summary: PARIS — France test-fired an upgraded version of its M51 strategic ballistic missile from a submarine for the first time on Tuesday, a capability demonstration that President Emmanuel Macron called “very important” for the country’s strategic credibility and which he said would be monitored by allies and adversaries alike. evidenceRecords.text: PARIS — France test-fired an upgraded version of its M51 strategic ballistic missile from a submarine for the first time on Tuesday, a capability demonstration that President Emmanuel Macron called “very important” for the country’s strategic credibility and which he said would be monitored by allies and adversaries alike.

Today’s launch was the seventh time a variant of the M51 was fired from a French submarine, and the 13th launch of the missile overall, all of them “of course, conducted without a nuclear warhead,” according to the ministry.
The nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine Le Vigilant fired an M51.3 missile in an acceptance test following the boat’s overhaul, the Ministry of the Armed Forces said in a statement.

The missile, which didn’t carry a nuclear warhead, was launched off Finistère in western France and splashed down in the North Atlantic several hundred kilometers from any coastline, the ministry said.
The first version of the M51 was fired from the Biscarrosse launch site in 2006, with the first submarine launch from the SSBN Le Terrible in January 2010.

Their robotics and test technologies are complementary to our platform, and together we can help customers simplify integration, accelerate deployment, and maintain a complete production data thread.” Partners share AI infrastructure experience AI infrastructure is driving one of the largest electronics manufacturing buildouts in recent history, noted Teradyne.

items.summary: Insider Brief Xanadu and GlobalFoundries have entered a multi-year partnership to develop and manufacture photonic components for utility-scale quantum computing. The companies plan to use the manufacturing platform for future photonic quantum modules and Xanadu ’s fault-tolerant quantum computing demonstrators.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Xanadu and GlobalFoundries have entered a multi-year partnership to develop and manufacture photonic components for utility-scale quantum computing.
The companies plan to use the manufacturing platform for future photonic quantum modules and Xanadu ’s fault-tolerant quantum computing demonstrators.

PRESS RELEASE — Xanadu Quantum Technologies Limited (“ Xanadu “; NASDAQ/TSX: XNDU), a leading photonic quantum computing company, today announced a strategic multi-year partnership with GlobalFoundries (GF), a leading semiconductor manufacturer, to address the high-volume production required for utility-scale quantum computing.

This partnership combines Xanadu’s existing expertise in ultra-low loss photonic design and process development with GF’s industry-leading photonics manufacturing prowess to accelerate the development and manufacturing of advanced photonic components, including ultra-low loss silicon nitride (SiN) photonics and Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detectors (SNSPDs), through GF’s 300 mm production line in Malta, New York.

The adoption of SNSPDs is expected to dramatically increase the speed of Xanadu’s quantum computing systems and considerably reduce the chip overheads needed to deliver utility-scale quantum computers with Xanadu’s photonic quantum computing architecture.

Combining ultra-high efficiency SNSPDs with ultra-low loss SiN photonics, used as optical circuit boards to guide photons with negligible signal loss across a wide spectrum of light, forms the backbone of Xanadu’s photonic quantum computing technology.

In addition to SNSPDs and SiN, Xanadu and GF are exploring future work packages to further develop high-performance quantum modules that are intended to increase the power and utility of photonic quantum computing systems.

The output of this collaboration is expected to serve as the manufacturing foundation for Xanadu’s upcoming fault-tolerant demonstrators, supporting the company’s long-term objective of providing the hardware architecture for future quantum data centers.
“Transitioning quantum computing technology to a high-volume manufacturing line is fundamental to delivering quantum computing at scale,” said Dr.
Christian Weedbrook, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Xanadu .

“Partnering with GlobalFoundries allows Xanadu to refine and scale up our existing industry-leading photonics platform and apply GF’s industrial expertise and technology to our photonic chip production.

This partnership demonstrates our focus on execution and seeks to provide the reliable, precision-manufactured infrastructure necessary to transition quantum technology from the research environment to commercial-scale data centers.” “By combining Xanadu ’s advanced photonic computing technology with GF’s 300 mm manufacturing expertise, this partnership creates a path to industrialize the critical components needed to accelerate the deployment of fault-tolerant systems and enable future quantum computing architectures,” said Nicholas Sergeant, VP of Quantum Technology Solutions at GF.

PRESS RELEASE — Pasqal (NASDAQ: PSQL), a global leader in neutral-atom quantum computing, is coordinating the implementation of Q-PLANET (Quantum Pilot Line for production of Advanced chips for Neutral atom European Technologies), co-funded by the EU Chips Joint Undertaking (Chips JU) and National/Regional authorities.

Backed by €50 million over three years, the consortium brings together 28 partners from 11 European countries to develop industrial-grade chip components for neutral-atom quantum computing, sensing, and communication.

A Concrete Commitment to Europe’s Quantum Industrial Ambitions and Strategic Autonomy Pasqal ’s leadership of Q-PLANET reflects the company’s concrete commitment to the European Union’s industrial quantum ambitions, in line with the upcoming EU Quantum Act.

Through Q-PLANET, Pasqal is delivering one of the flagship initiatives of the European Quantum Strategy, aimed at supporting the large-scale industrialization of quantum technologies across the European Union.

Strengthening Europe’s Neutral-atom Ecosystem & Building a European Quantum Market around User Needs Under Pasqal ’s leadership, Q-PLANET will strengthen the European industrial and scientific neutral-atom ecosystem by bringing together leading research and technology organizations, industry partners and academic research groups.

Together with our 28 partners, we are building a European supply chain for neutral-atom technologies, while bringing quantum industrialization closer to concrete user needs,” said Loïc Henriet, CTO of Pasqal .

“Q-PLANET reflects Pasqal’s commitment to Europe’s quantum ambitions, bridging large-scale industrialization rooted in resilient capabilities with real-world application to build a globally competitive and resilient European quantum industry.”

But two-year-old, San Francisco-based Mirror Particle thinks that approach is fundamentally broken.

“It’s like bringing a super soaker to Niagara Falls,” says Abhivyakti Ahuja, co-founder and CEO of Mirror Particle, which provides brands with an AI engine that predicts consumer behavior and the reasons behind it. “LLMs have been trained on hundreds of billions of data points.

items.title: Has the Pentagon given up on AI polygraph analysis of trustworthiness?
items.originalTitle: Has the Pentagon given up on AI polygraph analysis of trustworthiness?
items.summary: As of July, the Pentagon had been prepping artificial intelligence tools that analyze text, voices and faces to estimate trustworthiness, according to declassified presentation slides and prior Defense Department statements. Now, Pentagon officials say that some of that AI is not part of the current revamp of the polygraph interview process, after Defense News asked for a response to concerns about the earlier statements and the slides.

evidenceRecords.text: As of July, the Pentagon had been prepping artificial intelligence tools that analyze text, voices and faces to estimate trustworthiness, according to declassified presentation slides and prior Defense Department statements.

Now, Pentagon officials say that some of that AI is not part of the current revamp of the polygraph interview process, after Defense News asked for a response to concerns about the earlier statements and the slides.

On Wednesday, the Pentagon’s Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency, or DCSA, which vets security clearance holders and applicants, said in an emailed statement that “active research and development” for the “Modernizing Polygraph” effort “does not incorporate generative super intelligence , also known as artificial intelligence,” that creates new content — such as emails, graphics or voiceovers.
In July, a Pentagon official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the technology, explained the advantages of AI-driven sentiment and deception analysis.

On Friday, DCSA declined to provide additional information, including the scope of the “Modernizing Polygraph” project and the decision not to include AI-based voice screening and facial expression analysis.

In response to concerns about multimodal systems in July, the Pentagon official had said, “Any automated output is treated strictly as auxiliary data for a highly trained, certified polygraph examiner.”

In August, when the Pentagon administered a raft of polygraph exams to probe leaks alleging the Iran conflict is depleting U.S. arsenals, some observers suspected the endgame was not to find the leakers, but to crack down on disloyalty.
The expectations for AI-powered trustworthiness testing resemble the hope that U.S. national security officials held out for the polygraph about 100 years ago, other lawyers said.

evidenceRecords.text: If you’re looking for a document editor that doesn’t use artificial intelligence, LibreOffice may be just the software for you.

The Document Foundation, the nonprofit software maker behind the open source document editor LibreOffice, said in a blog post this week that while it does not reject AI out of hand, it “will not add” AI to its software for the foreseeable future.
The blog post comes weeks after the release of the latest version of LibreOffice in late August, in which the nonprofit reiterated that the software “contains no generative AI features.”

LibreOffice said at the time that this was a “deliberate design position” to ensure that users’ documents are not uploaded to a server for processing and that no part of the software requires a network connection to function.
The nonprofit added that its software is used by tens of millions of people and organizations, and that users should retain control over their data.
LibreOffice says users can still choose to use AI tools by installing software extensions that connect the document editor to local AI models.

LibreOffice said that there is currently “no integration” that meets all of its requirements, such as ensuring that the users’ data stays on their device and that there is no reliance on a single AI provider, among other considerations.

The organization’s criteria for including AI into its software is not a “definitive rejection,” but the decision was an assessment of the technology today, rather than a “judgement on the value of the sector.”
LibreOffice is one of the many kinds of open source and alternative software used to escape the clutches of Silicon Valley tech giants.

evidenceRecords.text: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory The Beaver Brown Waters of… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search The Cree word pahtaaunaakun seems particularly apt for describing the distinctive brown hues of the waters that drain into Hannah Bay and Rupert

Meaning the “color of singed beaver” in Southern East Cree , the word evokes the rich brown of the humic-substance-stained waters that were flowing into the two bays in late September 2026, as well as the role that beavers have long played in the mythology and history of the region.

When the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on September 27, 2026, the Moose, Nottaway, and Harricanaw rivers were carrying tea-colored water across the broad mudflats of Hannah and Rupert bays and mingling with the darker blue waters of James Bay.
The mudflats, the light brown areas along the shore, are a product of the shallow, sloping bathymetry in the southernmost part of James Bay.

European traders arrived in Rupert Bay as early as the 1660s to pursue the animals as well, leading to the establishment of several trading posts along the bay’s shores and the founding of the Hudson’s Bay Company to cultivate the fur trade, especially in beaver pelts.

For instance, one Cree myth about this area, recorded by the anthropologist Alanson Skinner , tells of a giant pursuing an enormous mythical beaver down the Nottaway River until the beaver escaped into Rupert Bay.

In an early example of a managed beaver preserve in Canada, the Hudson’s Bay Company worked with local Cree people in the 1830s and again a century later to set up Charlton Island as a place to raise beavers for later trapping.

Finding the right company or product in the rapidly expanding drone and mobile robot industry can be harder than it sounds.
There are thousands of specialized suppliers, but knowing which ones actually fit a particular requirement can take considerable research.

Drone Industry Insights (DII) is trying to make that process easier with ASTRA Intelligence, a new searchable platform designed to connect companies, products and services across the global mobile robot ecosystem.
ASTRA comes with several tools aimed at buyers, suppliers, investors, and policymakers.
One of the more interesting additions is a supply chain view that maps companies across different parts of the mobile robot ecosystem.
Users can see suppliers ranging from component manufacturers to integrated-system providers and service companies.
The feature is also designed to help organizations identify potential suppliers in specific regions.
DII says ASTRA was built using the same industry data and research that supports its market analyses and Drone Market Map.
According to DII’s Global Drone Industry Survey, acquiring customers has been the industry’s second-biggest challenge for three consecutive years.
At the same time, domestic politics and geopolitical tensions are encouraging companies to rethink their supply chains and look for regional alternatives.
ASTRA is designed to address both challenges by making specialized suppliers easier to discover while giving companies another way to connect directly with potential customers.
The name ASTRA stands for Automation, Safety, Transportation, Robotics and Applications — the areas DII sees as central to mobile robot deployment.

evidenceRecords.text: Exclusive: Guardian analysis finds more than 150,000 tonnes of fuel was shipped to Russian ports in July and August, some using sanctioned tankers Fuel is being shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers as Moscow scrambles for supplies amid the war in Ukraine, a move one expert said “undermines” Seoul’s public backing for Kyiv.

Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Fuel is being shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers as Moscow scrambles for supplies amid the war in Ukraine, a move one expert said “undermines” Seoul’s public backing for Kyiv.

“It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia”, said Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank. “This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”
But South Korea has long sought to balance its support for Ukraine with its desire to improve ties with Russia.
Throughout the war, Seoul has ruled out sending weapons directly to Ukraine, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war.
Moscow has signalled an interest in restoring relations with South Korea, including trade ties.
While the fuel trade involves vessels sanctioned by some of Seoul’s western partners, it does not appear to breach South Korean law.
South Korea’s own measures against Russia rely mainly on export controls on goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.

The shipments, however, risk making Seoul look like a weak link in western efforts to pressure Russia, as relations with Kyiv come under strain over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul says was meant to remain secret.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, says Moscow has been forced to import fuel products to feed the “Russian war machine”.

In August, Russia imported 368,000 tonnes of oil products by sea, more than seven times the previous month and the highest monthly total since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Kpler data analysed by CREA.
South Korea accounted for 112,000 tonnes, or 31%, of that amount, second only to India.

“It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia”, said Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank.
“This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”
A 2025 trade association survey found that nearly 80% of South Korean firms that had stopped exporting to Russia since the war began were open to resuming trade.
In March, as the war with Iran shut the strait of Hormuz, South Korea capped exports of certain fuels and imported Russian naphtha under a US sanctions waiver.

A spokesperson said: “The UK remains firmly committed to the effective monitoring of our sanctions and to working with international partners to increase economic pressure on Russia and reduce the revenues funding its illegal war against Ukraine.”

items.summary: The problem, known as "supercooled large droplet icing," occurs when aircraft fly through clouds containing unusually large drops of water that are very cold but remain liquid. When a plane passes through those drops, they can rapidly freeze to surfaces that are not protected from ice buildup. evidenceRecords.text: The problem, known as "supercooled large droplet icing," occurs when aircraft fly through clouds containing unusually large drops of water that are very cold but remain liquid.
When a plane passes through those drops, they can rapidly freeze to surfaces that are not protected from ice buildup.
But in rarer cases, clouds can contain supercooled large drops up to 2,000 microns in diameter (if you've ever been caught in freezing rain, you've encountered these droplets at ground level).
These much larger droplets can hit or splash onto areas farther aft on an aircraft, including areas behind conventional ice protection systems.
Companies in the aviation industry rely on engineering tools to help design their aircraft.
Current tools work well for typical clouds, but engineers have questions about how well they account for the physics of supercooled large drops.
To help answer those questions, NASA is working to enhance the equipment it uses to generate and measure experimental clouds for testing in the Icing Research Tunnel.

items.title: OpenAI will watermark ChatGPT text in the EU but makes it optional for API users worldwide
items.originalTitle: OpenAI will watermark ChatGPT text in the EU but makes it optional for API users worldwide
items.summary: OpenAI is adding invisible watermarks to ChatGPT text to comply with EU rules. Unlike Anthropic, it will let API customers worldwide turn them off. The EU AI Act reportedly requires AI providers to label generated text in a machine-readable format. OpenAI's answer is textGrain, a technology that embeds an invisible statistical signal in the model's word choices. It works much like Claude's SynthID watermark, which uses Google's open-source technology. OpenAI says it will turn on watermarking for ChatGPT and Codex users in the European Union over the coming weeks.

Forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen have recaptured several key areas around Bab al-Mandab strait from Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said on Monday.

However, the offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the south-western part of Yemen, taking the key town of Turbah in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward the strategic provincial capital of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.
The Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government fighting against the Houthis.
He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets as part of the ongoing campaign.

The new push sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
